issues.legal_issue: The protection against enforcing a charge against property transferred for consideration without notice applies to property purchased at an execution auction, notwithstanding the definition of transfer in the Transfer of Property Act.
material_facts: A decree had declared a charge over several properties, including the property later sold in execution.
The sale proclamation did not mention the charge.
The auction purchaser paid consideration for the judgment-debtor’s interest in the property and had no notice of the charge.
issues.conclusion: The Transfer of Property Act provisions governing charges apply to execution auction sales. Because the charge was omitted from the proclamation, it could not be enforced against the property in the hands of the auction purchaser.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(d), 5 and 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, read together, make section 100 applicable to execution transfers: section 2(d)’s express saving for Chapter IV prevails over the inter vivos definition in section 5. Under section 100, a charge cannot be enforced against property held by a transferee for consideration without notice. Order XXI rule 66(2)(e) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires the sale proclamation to state encumbrances as fairly and accurately as possible. The Court approved Nawal Kishore v. The Municipal Board, Agra, R. L. Nanadkeolvar v. Sultan Jehan, and Munna Singh Allah Singh v. Wasti Ram Saraf, and rejected the contrary views in Arumilli Surayya v. Pinisetti Venkataramanamma and Creet v. Ganga Ram Gool Raj.

rule.if: execution_auction_sale and property_subject_to_charge and charge_omitted_from_proclamation and purchaser_paid_consideration and purchaser_lacked_notice

predicates.execution_auction_sale: The property was sold by auction in execution of a decree.
predicates.property_subject_to_charge: A charge existed over the property sold.
predicates.charge_omitted_from_proclamation: The sale proclamation did not disclose the charge.
predicates.purchaser_paid_consideration: The auction purchaser gave consideration for acquiring the judgment-debtor’s interest in the property.
predicates.purchaser_lacked_notice: The auction purchaser had no notice of the charge.

issues.definition: When an execution auction transfers charged property for consideration to a purchaser without notice, omission of the charge from the proclamation means the charge cannot be enforced against that purchaser.

issues.legal_issue: An application to set aside an execution sale need not be dismissed for lack of an express averment of substantial injury when the pleaded material irregularity itself necessarily implies injury.
material_facts: The charge-holder applied under Order XXI rule 90 to set aside an execution sale.
The application alleged that the sale proclamation omitted a charge that had been declared over the property.
Because the charge was omitted and the purchaser had no notice, the charge-holder could not enforce the charge against the property in the purchaser’s hands.
The application did not expressly state that the irregularity caused substantial injury.
issues.conclusion: The application was not liable to dismissal merely because it lacked an express averment of substantial injury; in these circumstances, the injury could be implicit in the pleaded irregularity.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXI rule 90(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale and, under its proviso, substantial injury resulting from it. Although an applicant should allege both the irregularity and the injury, it is too technical to dismiss an application for want of an express injury averment where the alleged irregularity necessarily causes injury by making the charge unenforceable under section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.

rule.if: application_to_set_aside_execution_sale and material_irregularity_alleged and irregularity_makes_charge_unenforceable and no_express_injury_averment

predicates.application_to_set_aside_execution_sale: A person applied to set aside a property sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.material_irregularity_alleged: The applicant alleged a material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
predicates.irregularity_makes_charge_unenforceable: The alleged irregularity caused the applicant’s charge to become unenforceable against the purchaser of the property.
predicates.no_express_injury_averment: The application did not expressly aver that the irregularity caused substantial injury.

issues.definition: If an application challenging an execution sale alleges an irregularity that makes a charge unenforceable, the absence of a separate express injury averment does not by itself require dismissal.

issues.legal_issue: The loss of enforceability of a charge against an auction purchaser does not, by itself, establish substantial injury warranting the setting aside of an execution sale.
material_facts: The sale involved one of several properties subject to the charge.
Other properties remained available to the charge-holder, and the executing court found that their value was sufficient to meet the charge-holder’s legitimate maintenance claims.
While the appeal was pending, the charge-holder also acquired an interest in part of the remaining estate.
The High Court treated the loss of enforceability against the auction purchaser as sufficient, by itself, to establish substantial injury.
issues.conclusion: The charge-holder had not shown substantial injury because the remaining available properties were sufficient to meet her legitimate claims. The application to set aside the sale was dismissed and the High Court’s order was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to Order XXI rule 90(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires proof of substantial injury caused by the material irregularity or fraud; such injury is a question of fact and does not follow automatically from a charge becoming unenforceable against an auction purchaser. The court must consider relevant circumstances, including the properties sold, the properties subject to the charge, the extent of the claim, and the other assets available to satisfy it.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_execution_sale: A person applied to set aside a property sale conducted in execution of a decree.
predicates.charge_lost_enforceability_against_purch: The applicant’s charge could not be enforced against the property in the auction purchaser’s hands.
predicates.other_charged_properties_sufficient_to_m: Other properties subject to the charge remained available and were sufficient to meet the charge-holder’s legitimate claim.

issues.definition: When other charged properties available to the charge-holder are sufficient to meet the legitimate claim, loss of enforceability against the auction purchaser does not establish substantial injury and the application to set aside the sale is dismissed.
